# **Abstention-First Entity Resolution for Social and Media Catalogs**

In social networks and media catalogs, entity resolution (ER) operates under an acute cost asymmetry: a missed match merely leaves profiles or discographies fragmented, whereas a false merge corrupts the identity graph by mixing distinct individuals' histories, misallocating streaming royalties, displaying the wrong artist on playback surfaces, or uniting attacker-staged accounts with victim identities1. Because naive transitive closure propagates a single false-positive link across an entire connected component6, precision-critical systems must adopt an **abstention-first** architecture—treating *possible-match*, *unlinkable*, and explicit exclusion states as first-class outcomes rather than residual edge cases8.  
Comparing the three core paradigms clarifies a strict division of labor rather than a single winning model. **Fellegi–Sunter (F–S) engines such as Splink** deliver transparent, additive log-odds scoring and term-frequency adjustments at high batch throughput (reported at 9.24 seconds for 1 million synthetic records on DuckDB in a vendor benchmark, and roughly a minute on a laptop in state health practice), yet their conditional independence assumption double-counts correlated attributes, their EM parameter estimates can miscalibrate posterior probabilities, and their SQL blocking rules set a hard ceiling on recall6. **Evidence-weighted bipartite and signed graph clustering** curbs transitive "mega-clusters" by enforcing 1-to-1 clean-source exclusivity, explicit negative (non-merge) boundaries, Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) discography cuts, and verified cross-cluster checks, though batch clustering remains fragile when underlying pairwise precision is low7. **Selective classification and confidence calibration**—combining parametric recalibration (Platt or Beta scaling) with Neyman–Pearson error bounds and Conformal Risk Control (CRC)—separates score ranking from error control, bounding expected false-merge risk under statistical exchangeability or stability conditions while isolating ambiguous records in a blinded human-review queue11.  
Even an optimal static pipeline will suffer systematic false merges in social and media domains unless it addresses three dynamic hazards: **temporal handle drift** (where recycled, squatted, or hijacked usernames invalidate static string equality over time)25, **alias collisions** (homonymous artists, covers, and sparse metadata profiles requiring multi-modal audio/graph signals and authoritative identifiers like ISNI and MBID)1, and **retroactive cluster repair** (requiring reversible, append-only merge/split audit logs because any online correlation clustering algorithm achieving a constant-factor approximation mathematically incurs ![][image1] cluster recourse as new records arrive)5.

## **Comparative Architecture: Scoring, Graph Partitioning, and Abstention**

High-precision catalog resolution decouples candidate generation (blocking), pairwise evidence scoring, global cluster partitioning, and risk-bounded abstention so no single failure mode dictates a merge10.

| Architectural Layer | Representative Methods | Primary Operational Strength | Core False-Merge Failure Mode | Scalability and Complexity | Role in Abstention-First Stack |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Probabilistic Pairwise Scoring** | Fellegi–Sunter and extensions (Splink, FastLink, BRL, FlexRL)33 | Explainable additive log-odds weights; unsupervised EM training; high DuckDB/Spark throughput6 | Conditional independence double-counts correlated fields; naive posterior probabilities underestimate false discovery13 | Bounded by blocking; Splink linked 1M records in 9.24s on DuckDB (vendor benchmark)6 | Produces interpretable per-feature evidence weights and candidate scores; unsafe as an uncalibrated auto-merge gate6 |
| **Evidence-Weighted Bipartite and Signed Clustering** | UMC / FAMER CLIP, EXC, RCA, BAH, Correlation Clustering, MST cuts, Verified Merge7 | Enforces 1-to-1 clean-source exclusivity; blocks transitive bridges via negative edges and cross-cluster verification7 | Naive connected components (CNC) lets sparse records bridge dense clusters into mega-clusters6 | CNC ![][image2]; UMC/CLIP ![][image3]; EXC ![][image4]; RCA ![][image5]; Hungarian ![][image6]16 | Resolves global conflicts, enforces hard exclusions, and halts ambiguous bridges before merge7 |
| **Selective Calibration and Risk Control** | Beta, Platt, and Isotonic calibration; Selective Calibration; Neyman–Pearson (NP); Conformal Risk Control (CRC / SCRC)10 | Decouples discrimination from error control; supports prior-free Type I bounds (NP) and finite-sample risk guarantees (CRC)21 | Calibrating solely on score-triggered review queues leaves risk unidentifiable in silent sub-threshold bands39 | Low scoring overhead (1–3 params for Temp/Platt/Beta); requires held-out calibration and random audit data23 | Calibrates upper/lower cutoffs (![][image7]) that protect auto-merges and route middle-band pairs to SMEs10 |

### **Fellegi–Sunter Models and Splink Under False-Merge Constraints**

Grounded in Fellegi and Sunter (1969), probabilistic record linkage evaluates a comparison vector ![][image8] across ![][image9] fields to classify record pairs into matches (![][image10]), non-matches (![][image11]), and a middle grey zone held for clerical review40. For each field comparison level, the model tracks ![][image12] (observing that level among true matches, reflecting data reliability) and ![][image13] (observing it by coincidence among non-matches), anchored by the prior match probability ![][image14]12. Under conditional independence, total evidence sums additively in ![][image15] match weights12:  
![][image16]  
Splink converts ![][image17] into a posterior match probability via ![][image18]; in Splink's documentation, match weights of 0, 4, 7, and 9.48 correspond to approximate match probabilities of 0.50, 0.95, 0.99, and 0.99912. Crucially, **term frequency (TF) adjustments** replace average non-match coincidence rates with token-specific frequencies—down-weighting common surnames like *Smith* or *Jovanović* while boosting rare tokens like *Žarković*6. Empirical evaluation of frequency-based weight adjustments confirmed meaningful discrimination gains on skewed linking keys, lifting Area Under the Curve (AUC) from 0.806 to 0.835 on a telephone-blocked scheme and from 0.818 to 0.831 on a name-blocked scheme44.  
Despite Splink's transparent waterfall diagnostics and SQL execution over DuckDB, Spark, or Athena6, five structural limitations prevent raw F–S probabilities from acting as autonomous merge triggers where false merges are unacceptable. First, **correlated fields break conditional independence**: attributes such as genre, music label, language, and collaborator lists—or street, city, and postcode—co-vary strongly, causing additive weights to count identical evidence repeatedly and bias parameter estimates13. A technical review by Zingg citing Xu, Li, and Grannis (*JRSS Series C*, 2022\) notes that ignoring dependence biases estimated parameters, misspecifying dependence models can degrade linkage further, and standard dependence diagnostics often fail13. Combining correlated fields into compound comparisons in Splink reduces double-counting45, yet expanding multinomial comparison cells increases computational burden and can destabilize EM convergence46.  
Second, **TF adjustments carry hidden assumptions on fuzzy and multi-valued fields**. Splink engineering discussions highlight that exact-match TF scaling implicitly assumes ![][image19]—meaning duplication rates are assumed equal regardless of name frequency—and applying TF corrections to fuzzy similarity levels (such as Levenshtein distance) risks conflating distinct legitimate names (e.g., *Johnson* vs. *Johnston*) rather than genuine typos, while multi-valued arrays require heuristic anchoring43. Third, **unsupervised EM estimation is sensitive to initialization and priors**: EM converges only to local likelihood maxima, and in a production UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) Demographic Index linkage of 57,917,164 records (match proportion 0.007) using Splink \< v3, engineers found that while ![][image20] values were estimated reliably via random sampling, ![][image21] values were problematic to estimate automatically and required extensive tuning, with prior (![][image22]) shifts directly altering downstream scores13.  
Fourth, **classical error estimators underestimate false discoveries**. Traditional unsupervised false-match calibration via Belin and Rubin (1995) works well only under narrow conditions approximating conditional independence and 1-to-1 matching41. A 2025 study applying target-decoy synthetic augmentation to SPLink outputs demonstrated that standard probabilistic False Discovery Proportion (FDP) estimates are substantially biased downward, whereas a decoy-augmented estimator bounded FDP estimation bias within 20%34. Fifth, **blocking rules bound recall while supervised models exploit richer structure**. Because Splink only scores candidate pairs generated by SQL blocking expressions, duplicates whose blocking keys are both corrupted suffer silent false negatives6. In a vendor-published synthetic benchmark (Tilores, 1,000,000 records with 100,000 true duplicate pairs), Splink achieved F1 0.8867 (recall 0.7965, 79,655 TP, 20,345 FN) versus Tilores's rule-graph F1 0.9949 (recall 0.9900, 99,000 TP, 1,000 FN), though Splink produced three times fewer false positives (5 vs. 15\) and completed in 9.24 seconds on DuckDB15. When representative labeled pairs exist, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2018) and ONS 2021 Census evaluations cited in the Zingg review show supervised classifiers (gradient boosting, random forests, SVMs, logistic regression) outperforming F–S baselines by capturing feature interactions and single-source missingness, while Bayesian alternatives like BRL model cross-pair dependencies via Gibbs sampling at substantially higher memory cost13.

### **Evidence-Weighted Bipartite and Signed Graph Clustering**

Pairwise classification leaves unresolved how overlapping scores reconcile globally across multi-record neighborhoods6. Applying naive **Connected Components (CNC)** above a threshold ![][image23] performs transitive closure, allowing a single sparse profile—such as an artist stub carrying only a common stage name—to act as a bridge linking two otherwise unrelated entities that were never directly compared6. A 2026 evaluation of a self-serve ER engine across six benchmarks (864 to 5 million records) found that transitivity is generally safe only when baseline pairwise precision exceeds 0.9, whereas below 0.5 it reliably collapses records into giant "mega-clusters"7.  
Graph-based clustering mitigates transitive collapse through three complementary structural constraints. When reconciling two internally deduplicated catalogs ![][image24] and ![][image25]—such as MusicBrainz and Spotify artist tables—the task becomes **Clean-Clean ER (CCER)** on a weighted bipartite graph ![][image26], where valid clusters contain at most one node per source16. In Papadakis et al.'s EDBT 2022 empirical evaluation of bipartite algorithms (all maintaining ![][image27] space complexity, with ![][image28] and ![][image29]), CNC runs in ![][image2] time but discards every component whose size is not 2, losing valid matches whenever a single noisy edge creates a larger component32. Instead, **Unique Mapping Clustering (UMC)**—equivalent in CCER to the **CLIP** algorithm in the **FAMER** multi-source framework—sorts edges above ![][image23] in descending similarity and locks pairs greedily in ![][image3] time so neither entity can match twice16. Stricter symmetric pruning via **Exact Clustering (EXC)** (![][image4]) enforces reciprocal top choices, while **Row-Column Assignment (RCA)** (![][image30]) and the swap-based **Best Assignment Heuristic (BAH)** approximate maximum-weight bipartite matching without the prohibitive ![][image6] cost of the exact Hungarian algorithm16. Across more than two clean sources, FAMER generalizes these constraints via **source-consistency filtering** (forbidding two records from the same clean source within one cluster) and **max-both** reciprocal assignment17.  
Beyond source exclusivity, precision-critical catalogs require explicit contradiction modeling via **signed graph correlation clustering**18. Formalized by Bansal, Blum, and Chawla (2004), correlation clustering partitions a signed graph ![][image31] to minimize weighted disagreements—penalizing negative edges inside clusters and positive edges cut across clusters—without fixing cluster count ![][image32] in advance18. In media and social catalogs, negative (![][image33]) edges encode contradictory exclusive attributes (incompatible ISNIs, non-overlapping lifespans, generational suffixes like I vs. II flagged by Senzing's \-GENERATION check, divergent acoustic signatures, or persistent manual rejections)19. Because unweighted or finite-weight correlation clustering can theoretically leave a negative edge inside an optimal cluster when surrounding triangle disagreements dominate18, hard domain invariants (such as conflicting authoritative IDs or human split overrides) must act as absolute merge vetoes rather than soft weights.  
Finally, **structural verification and tree-cut algorithms** protect against bridge collapse and artistic drift simultaneously. **Verified Merge** clustering forces direct pairwise comparison between non-adjacent members of two candidate clusters whenever a merge is proposed, immediately blocking bridges mediated solely by a sparse node7. In production music curation, Spotify's **"Which Witch"** pipeline (November 2023\) addresses intra-discography pollution—where homonymous artists share one profile—by computing pairwise release distances, constructing a **Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)**, and severing edges whose distance exceeds a threshold19. Because an MST connects chronologically or stylistically adjacent releases, a legitimate artist's gradual evolution across albums remains intact while disconnected homonym releases cleanly split before cross-catalog duplicate merging runs19.

### **Selective Classification, Confidence Calibration, and Human-Review Queues**

Because raw model scores reflect ranking power (ROC-AUC) rather than true match probability, threshold selection cannot rely on uncalibrated outputs13. Post-hoc calibration must be fit on a **held-out calibration split** never seen during training—and evaluated with reliability diagrams and log-loss alongside Expected Calibration Error (ECE), mindful of ECE's sensitivity to bin placement23.

| Calibration Method | Transformation and Parameters | Minimum Calibration Samples (NNN) | Distortion Fit and AUC Impact | Primary Failure Mode in Catalog ER |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Platt Scaling**23 | Logistic fit on score ![][image34]: ![][image35] (2 params)23 | Small (\~50 minimum; 200–1,000 typical)23 | Strictly monotonic (preserves ROC-AUC)56 | Assumes symmetric equal-variance Gaussian scores; misfits heavily imbalanced ER distributions56 |
| **Beta Calibration**23 | Logistic fit on ![][image36] and ![][image37] (3 params: ![][image38])23 | Small–Moderate (\~100–200 in technical benchmark)23 | Smooth; contains identity (![][image39]); fits skewed ensemble scores; may slightly affect AUC23 | Rare parametric misfit on strongly multi-modal score shapes23 |
| **Isotonic Regression**23 | Piecewise-constant non-decreasing PAVA fit (![][image40] steps)23 | Large (≥ 1,000 in scikit-learn; ≥ 1,000–5,000 per CASRAI)56 | Fits arbitrary monotonic curves; introduces probability ties that can alter AUC56 | Severe overfitting and jagged step boundaries on scarce gold-standard ER labels, harming extreme ![][image41] precision23 |
| **Temperature Scaling**56 | Divides neural logits by scalar ![][image42] before softmax (1 param)56 | Very small58 | Preserves argmax and ranking; native multiclass (match / related / non-match)56 | Applies only to logit vectors; single scalar cannot correct complex non-monotonic or asymmetric calibration errors56 |

For binary pairwise ER with limited gold labels (100–500 pairs), a calibration benchmark suggests **Beta calibration** captures skewed tree and Fellegi–Sunter score curves with far lower variance than isotonic regression, while **Platt scaling** remains the safer choice below \~100 pairs and **Isotonic regression** requires ≥ 1,000–5,000 independent labeled pairs to stabilize tail probabilities23.  
To guarantee error bounds under distribution shift and severe class imbalance, calibrated scores feed into selective abstention gates. **Selective Calibration** (Fisch, Jaakkola, and Barzilay, TMLR 2022\) trains a dedicated selector network with distributionally robust input perturbations to abstain whenever an input exhibits "uncertain uncertainties"—preventing unfamiliar catalog slices (e.g., newly ingested international catalogs) from producing high-confidence false merges20. To enforce explicit operational tolerances (![][image43] auto-merge, ![][image44] clerical review, ![][image45] auto-non-match)40, two statistical paradigms provide formal cutoffs:

* **Neyman–Pearson (NP) Classification with Indecisions:** Standard NP classification minimizes false negatives subject to a strict false-positive constraint ![][image46] **without assuming training match priors equal deployment priors**—vital in ER because blocking keys alter match prevalence across cohorts24. Recent extensions ("NP Classification with Indecisions," 2026\) introduce an explicit abstention band to simultaneously bound selective Type I and Type II errors61.  
* **Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and Selective CRC:** Generalizing split conformal prediction, CRC (Angelopoulos et al., ICLR 2024\) selects a threshold ![][image47] over ![][image48] exchangeable calibration samples so expected monotone loss obeys ![][image49] up to an ![][image50] slack21. Recent 2026 extensions establish finite-sample stability bounds for non-monotonic selective classification losses22 and introduce two-stage **Selective CRC (SCRC-T, SCRC-I)**, pairing an abstention gate ![][image51] (controlling coverage ![][image52]) with a risk gate ![][image53] (controlling conditional error ![][image54])10.

A critical operational caveat governs calibration data collection: **thresholded-event selection bias**39. Because human reviewers normally annotate only pairs crossing ![][image55], queue-derived datasets systematically omit sub-threshold records and correlate labeling with past model scores, rendering population risk unidentifiable under temporal dependence39. A 2026 study in *Axioms* demonstrates that restoring valid risk guarantees requires supplementing queue labels with a small **auxiliary random audit stream** sampled across the silent sub-threshold region39.  
Empirical deployments prove that human review remains a permanent operational tier rather than a temporary phase. In Spotify's "Which Witch" SME evaluation (\~1,000 examples each for misattribution and duplication), tuning both Random Forest sub-models to high confidence thresholds yielded a maximum end-to-end relocation precision of **45% (covering 17% of the sample)**—highly valuable for guiding curators to candidate destination discographies without manual search, yet unsafe for unsupervised auto-merging19. Likewise, a 12-million-record linkage evaluation by Azimaee et al. (IJPDS 2024, cited in the Zingg review) identified grey-zone clerical review as the most resource-intensive and error-prone linkage stage, while a Brazilian dengue and stillbirth linkage study cited in the same review saw positive predictive value plunge from **92.5% to 68.4%** for only a **4.7 percentage-point gain in sensitivity** (64.4% to 69.1%) when loosening a single threshold13.  
Effective abstention queues follow three operational rules derived from production implementations. First, **bundle rich disambiguating context**: in twiddle\#45 (October 2026 live-music dataset containing 209 name\_only and 176 multi-candidate uncertain bands, with 60 ambiguous queue items having multiple Spotify candidates), retaining only id, name, and genres (frequently empty) left reviewers unable to separate homonyms like *Amardeep* (2 candidates) or *Angel White* (3 candidates)1. Adding follower counts, popularity, top tracks/albums, Bandcamp/MusicBrainz links, and billing metadata (venue, city, date, co-billed acts) enables confident picks where evidence aligns while keeping genuine ties like *Angel White* in uncertain1. Second, **blind reviewers to model probabilities**: Splink exposes show\_splink\_predictions\_in\_interface=False specifically to prevent anchoring bias during clerical labeling11. Third, **separate structurally unlinkable stubs from genuine conflicts**: Splink's unlinkables diagnostic isolates records lacking enough attribute entropy to confirm a match even against themselves, allowing systems to route sparse stubs to metadata enrichment instead of exhausting human reviewers11.

## **Domain-Specific Failure Modes in Social and Media Catalogs**

### **Temporal Handle Drift, Recycling, and Account Takeovers**

Social identifiers decay over time. Formal **temporal record linkage** (Dong, Li, and Chiang, PVLDB 2011 / VLDB 2014\) models two inverse failure mechanisms across elapsed time ![][image56]25. **Within-entity temporal disagreement** occurs when a user rebrands or migrates handles, modeled via **disagreement decay** ![][image57]—the probability an entity mutates attribute ![][image58] within ![][image56]—so attribute mismatch across long gaps imposes smaller penalties25. Conversely, **between-entity temporal agreement** occurs when a new account acquires an attribute previously held by a different entity, modeled via **agreement decay** ![][image59]—requiring systems to discount the positive match weight of volatile handles across time intervals25.  
Real platform mechanics convert static handle matching into an acute security and false-merge hazard. When a GitHub user renames an account, GitHub creates automatic redirects from the old handle, which persist only until another user claims that handle (subject to a 90-day hold period described in GitHub community discussions, alongside retired-namespace protections for popular repositories that Checkmarx researchers showed could still be targeted via Repojacking race conditions before patching)27. Similarly, a vendor guide on username claiming notes that TikTok reserves the right to reset usernames after 180 days of inactivity while X and Instagram purge inactive handles without fixed public schedules65. Account takeovers compound drift with adversarial spoofing: Constella's 2026 Identity Breach Report (vendor threat intelligence) notes that nearly 60% of breach compilations recycle exposed credentials alongside session-cookie infostealers, while Specops (vendor blog) attributes 22% of 2025 breaches to credential abuse66. Attackers who compromise GitHub accounts (e.g., a campaign targeting 4,837 accounts to probe 61,764 repositories) routinely rename handles, rewrite commit histories, and scrub workflow logs68. Even without password theft, **OAuth pre-hijacking** (such as GHSA-29rf-f4vv-pvq6 in Authorizer and cases analyzed by Microsoft MSRC) enables an attacker to stage an unverified account under a victim's email; if the platform auto-merges profiles on email when the victim later completes OAuth login, both parties become permanently bound to one resolved identity4.  
Defending social catalogs against temporal drift and takeover contamination requires four structural controls:

> 1. **Anchor entities on immutable identifiers rather than mutable handles:** Adopting the **AT Protocol** model, represent canonical identity nodes via persistent cryptographic identifiers (such as W3C DIDs) while treating handles as mutable, case-normalized DNS labels (excluding disallowed local/onion TLDs)73.  
> 2. **Enforce bidirectional verification on every handle claim:** Following AT Protocol's HandleResolver and ActivityPub/WebFinger rel="me" safeguards, never trust a handle-to-identity or cross-domain rel="me" link unless *both* endpoints mutually confirm the binding (e.g., DNS \_atproto TXT or HTTPS /.well-known/ mapping handle ![][image60] DID *and* the DID document claiming the handle); broken links must resolve explicitly to handle.invalid rather than falling back to stale caches74.  
> 3. **Apply "unlink by default" on federated account linking:** Reject automatic merges between verified OAuth logins and pre-existing unverified accounts, invalidate prior password and session tokens upon external identity linkage, and require explicit user confirmation to retain linked endpoints4.  
> 4. **Treat anomalous multi-signal shifts as temporal discontinuities:** When a handle rename coincides with anomalous security telemetry—such as abrupt IP/device changes, rapid repository renames, or disabled branch protections68—halt automated cross-time merging via temporal decay gating25 and route the epoch boundary to human security/catalog review.

### **Alias Collisions, Homonyms, and Multi-Modal Disambiguation**

String similarity is structurally insufficient for media catalogs because distinct creators and recordings routinely share identical names. MusicBrainz documents prominent homonyms requiring explicit disambiguation strings—such as *John Williams* (film composer vs. classical guitarist) and *Randy Jackson* (brother of Michael and Janet vs. Journey bassist), plus homonymous releases like *"99 Red Balloons"* (Nena vs. Goldfinger)30. Even structured catalog codes display substantial 1-to-many branching: a 2025 personal catalog engineering benchmark matching Spotify tracks to MusicBrainz via ISRC and names mapped 2,010 matched tracks (out of 4,781 input tracks) to **8,172 recordings (7,105 unique)**, and a subsequent case-insensitive pass matched 12,333 tracks to **21,376 recordings (17,806 unique)**79. In commercial streaming catalogs, lexical blocking yields tight homonym neighborhoods like *Prince*, *Princess*, and *Prince of Funk*19, while event and venue scraping produces sparse local bands whose genre fields are blank1.  
High-precision alias resolution integrates three layered signals. First, **authoritative persistent identifiers strictly outrank lexical strings**: **ISNI** and **MBID** disambiguate artists and labels, **IPI** identifies rights holders, **ISWC** identifies underlying musical works, and **ISRC** (CCXXXYYNNNNN) identifies specific audio recordings—though practitioners must avoid merging distinct artists solely because they covered or appeared on matching recording/work strings2. Second, **multi-modal acoustic and metadata models cross-validate each other**: Spotify's "Which Witch" ablation experiments established that mel-spectrogram CNN audio embeddings primarily drive misattribution detection (splitting polluted artist pages), with metadata adding \+2% Average Precision (AP), whereas metadata attributes (collaborator overlap, performance language, music label) primarily drive duplicate detection (merging split discographies), with audio embeddings boosting AP by **\+6%**19. Third, **relational neighborhood overlap** resolves sparse stubs where text fails: checking shared collaborators, recording credits, external Bandcamp/Wikidata pages, and co-billed venue rosters transforms isolated name matches into verifiable graph evidence1.

## **Reversible Append-Only Merge/Split Audit Logs and Operational Governance**

Static, destructive table merges are fundamentally incompatible with streaming catalogs. Cohen-Addad et al. (ICML 2022\) proved that any online correlation clustering algorithm achieving a constant-factor competitive ratio must incur at least an ![][image1] recourse lower bound in cluster reassignments as vertices arrive31. Retroactive merges and splits are therefore a mathematical inevitability whenever delayed disambiguating evidence or human corrections arrive—making reversibility, provenance retention, and localized replay mandatory design requirements5.  
Synthesizing the enterprise audit control guidance in *Entity Resolution Under Audit* (a 2026 data-engineering framework by Logiciel)5 with operational designs from MusicBrainz30, Senzing52, FAMER17, Prometheux84, and Twiddle1 yields five concrete governance invariants:

* **Versioned input and model provenance:** Preserve immutable raw source records and bind every linkage decision to exact versions of blocking rules, normalization transforms, comparison vectors, F–S/ML model weights, and calibration thresholds so incident teams can reconstruct exact production decisions5.  
* **Append-only decision ledger with permanent redirects:** Materialize canonical entities as views over an append-only log of match assertions, negative exclusions, human-review holds, manual merges, manual splits, and sticky overrides—recording reviewer identity, timestamp, and rationale1. When canonical identifiers collapse—mirroring MusicBrainz MBID merges30—preserve retired IDs as permanent redirects while keeping underlying member pointers intact so subsequent splits cleanly unbind records5. (Note: While the reviewed engineering literature specifies these audit-control invariants, provenance chase graphs, and split/replay capabilities5, it does not prescribe a standardized database DDL or report empirical storage and query-latency overhead benchmarks for append-only ER audit ledgers.)  
* **Deterministic human-override precedence:** Adjudicated human splits and exclusions must persist across batch refreshes, as implemented via manual overrides in the UK Ministry of Justice's Splink pipeline54. Likewise, Twiddle's catalog build enforces strict precedence where a user pin unconditionally overrides an algorithmic or producer pick, and an inferred pick is barred from elevating a cluster's status to corroborated1.  
* **Neighborhood-scoped split and replay (n-depth reclustering):** Rather than re-running global batch clustering on tens of millions of nodes after a correction, FAMER's **n-depth reclustering (nDR)** extracts the ![][image48]\-hop similarity subgraph around newly added or impacted entities, repairs clusters locally using max-both and source-consistency constraints, and matches full batch quality independently of record arrival order17. Senzing similarly delivers sequence-neutral incremental updates alongside why and how commands for step-by-step path inspection52.  
* **Embargoed key propagation and continuous truth-set auditing:** Downstream consumers (royalty payouts, public discographies, analytics) must ingest canonical IDs only after threshold or review clearance5. Production governance should pair continuous truth-set audits—such as Senzing's sz\_audit, tracking within-source and cross-source MERGE (new positives) vs. SPLIT (new negatives) discrepancies52—with routine random sampling of both cleared merges and silent sub-threshold pairs5.

## **Recommended Reference Pipeline for High-Precision Catalogs**

Implementing an abstention-first ER pipeline for social and media catalogs requires ordering these mechanisms sequentially so each stage guards against the blind spots of its predecessor:

> 1. **Canonical Normalization and Cryptographic Anchor Extraction:** Standardize casing, diacritics, scripts, and null tokens before scoring so formatting mismatches or placeholder strings (N/A) do not distort ![][image21]/![][image20] estimates6. Extract immutable anchors—verified DIDs with bidirectional handle proofs74, mutually verified rel="me" links75, ISNI/IPI/ISWC/MBID identifiers2, and record timestamps—prior to string matching.  
> 2. **Multi-Strategy Recall-Preserving Blocking:** Pair overlapping Splink SQL blocking rules, Elasticsearch homonym/phonetic indexes, or Locality Sensitive Hashing with block-size diagnostics (verifyBlocking) to bound false negatives without generating unmanageable candidate blocks6.  
> 3. **Multi-Modal Scoring and Negative Edge Extraction:** Score candidates using compound Fellegi–Sunter comparisons (mitigating correlated-field double-counting)13 or supervised Random Forest / gradient-boosted models fusing metadata with mel-spectrogram CNN embeddings and collaborator-graph overlap13. Simultaneously emit time-decayed or hard negative (![][image33]) exclusion edges for conflicting ISNIs, incompatible eras/generations, same-source duplicates, and ATO/handle-change anomalies17.  
> 4. **Calibrated Selective Gate (NP / SCRC):** Fit a held-out **Beta calibrator** (or Isotonic regressor if ≥ 1,000–5,000 independent labeled pairs exist)23, and set upper/lower abstention thresholds (![][image7]) via Neyman–Pearson or Selective Conformal Risk Control fed by both queue feedback and a random silent-band audit stream10.  
> 5. **Signed Bipartite Clustering with Verified Merge and MST Cuts:** Resolve bipartite clean-source matches via UMC/CLIP and multi-source signed neighborhoods via correlation clustering enforcing hard exclusions16. Run **Verified Merge** cross-cluster checks and **MST edge-cutting** on artist discographies to sever sparse bridges prior to cluster commitment7.  
> 6. **Blinded Human-Review Queue and Append-Only Commit:** Route gray-zone pairs and blocked bridges to SMEs with full external, acoustic, billing, and temporal context while suppressing raw model scores1. Record every merge, split, and exclusion in an append-only provenance ledger where human overrides outrank automated inferences and trigger localized nDR reclustering upon split1.
